description: A mutual visa waiver dating to 1974 let citizens of either country visit the other without a visa. Migration increased notably from 1989.

After the Iran-Iraq war ended in 1988, many young Iranian men returning from the battlefields could not find work in Iran. Nearly 50,000 entered Japan in 1991, most as tourists permitted three months, and almost all went straight into small factories and service work that young Japanese avoided.
energy_note: Demobilised at 22 with no job and an open border.

description: With little Japanese and no established community to guide them, workers used Yoyogi and Ueno parks in central Tokyo to exchange news about work and housing. Thousands gathered at weekends; a 1993 report described Yoyogi as resembling 'a Middle Eastern bazaar'.
energy_note: A community improvised in a public park because there was nowhere else.

description: Unlike Chinese or Korean migrants, Iranians were easily recognised as foreigners, which made foreign labour a visible reality for Japanese society - and made them the face of it.
energy_note: Singled out for not blending in.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the numbers, and the cancellation
description: Illegal Iranian residents went from 764 in 1990 to 10,915 in 1991 to 40,001 in 1992. The waiver was cancelled in spring 1992 as overstays passed 40,000; with help from Tehran's embassy the number fell by more than 7,000 between May and November. By 2001 it was about 4,300.
energy_note: A population of 40,000 legislated down to 4,000.

aspect: The minority that defined the majority
description: A small minority turned to selling fake phone cards or drugs in the parks, and that became the focus of most press coverage - the standard mechanism by which a whole migrant cohort acquires a reputation.
energy_note: Judged by the worst of you, reported by the loudest.
